discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A series of systems will bring widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and increase the potential for coastal flooding along with high surf throughout much of the upcoming week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A series of systems will bring widespread precipitation, gusty winds, and increase the potential for coastal flooding along with high surf throughout much of the upcoming week.

sections.title: Short term (today through Wednesday)
paragraphs: Recent radar imagery shows a bulk of showers moving onshore early this morning, with most of the precipitation focused on the Olympic Peninsula. An upper level low will continue to meander offshore, providing shower activity throughout the early afternoon. A Coastal Flood Warning remains in effect for the coastline in Grays Harbor county where larger waves and lower pressure will most likely bring moderate to major coastal flooding, during this morning's hide tide, especially to places like Westport and Ocean Shores. Additionally, a Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect for the north coast and along the Strait of Juan De fuca, for minor coastal flooding this morning and afternoon. Snow levels generally hovering around 2000 to 3000 feet through this afternoon, where notable accumulation's are expected in the Olympics, around 4 to 8 inches. A Winter Weather Advisory remains in effect until early evening, where snow levels will rise to 3000 to 4500 feet.

A frontal system will start to move into the area late this evening into Tuesday, spreading widespread rainfall across the region. Along with rain, snow levels will gradually rise from 3000 to 4500 feet late this evening to generally around 5000 feet into Tuesday. Snow accumulations may be possible at the higher passes such as Stevens Pass, generally around 1 to 3 inches. Areas in the North Cascades, like Washington pass, could see 4 to 8 inches of snow, therefore a Winter Weather Advisory remains in effect through Tuesday.

Additionally, winds will become gusty across the region, with gusts up to 40 mph likely across areas along the coast, where a Wind Advisory remains through Tuesday afternoon. Precipitation will taper throughout the afternoon, with high temperatures in the low 50s. The tides increase more significantly for the Strait and Puget Sound coastlines later in the week around Tuesday onward, and the potential for impacts in these locations will need to be closely monitored as we get into the range of total water level guidance.
The active weather pattern continues, with yet another frontal system moving into the area Wednesday into Thursday with more batches of widespread lowland rain, breezy winds, and mountain snow.

sections.title: Long term (Wednesday night through Sunday)
paragraphs: Latest ensembles continue to highlight heavier rainfall Wednesday night into Thursday, especially over the Olympics, where the Skokomish River is forecasted to reach moderate flood stage. Confidence continues to increase for the potential of moderate to major coastal flooding stages being reached along portions of the Grays Harbor County coastline during Wednesday tides, with high surf possibly enhancing these impacts. We will continue to monitor this system as it gets closer with new model guidance.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A warm front will pass through the terminals this morning with a low pressure centered off the coast. The cold front will follow later today with another frontal system trailing into Tuesday. Bands of rain will continue to push north this morning, with a break in the interior later this morning, and rain continuing along the coast into the afternoon. The next system brings more widespread rain inland tonight/Tuesday. Visibility reductions down to MVFR are possible with the heaviest bands of rain. Ceilings are likely to remain VFR through tonight. MVFR chances increases for most terminals after 09Z through 15Z, with VFR returning later. Mountains likely see lower ceiling obstructions. Southeast winds will continue, with most seeing 5-10 kt, and higher gusts in the mountains and along the coast (approaching 30 kt and the Pacific coast seeing 35-40 kt most of Tuesday). Winds aloft will be stronger and out of the southwest, so there will be some potential for wind shear (especially Tuesday morning).

KSEA...VFR conditions anticipated for today, with a 30-40% chance of MVFR Tuesday morning from 09Z-12Z. Rain showers with the first round will continue through 15Z, with the next wave coming in after 00Z this evening. Winds stay out of the southeast 5-10 kt. Few gusts to 20 kt may mix in (especially Tuesday morning).
HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Low pressure will remain offshore for much of the week, with several fronts moving through the waters. The first front is moving through the waters this morning, and southeast winds will increase through the day today into Tuesday with the combo of systems passing through. Greatest impact (in terms of wind) remains the outer coastal waters, where a storm warning will go into effect for gusts up to 55 kt. The inner coastal waters and east Strait of Juan de Fuca areas have gale warnings, with  wind gusts up to 40 kt. There are also small craft advisories for adjacent areas of the central/west strait, northern inland waters and the Admiralty Inlet, where some sheltering from land will keep winds down to 20-30 kt.

Another frontal system will pass through Wednesday into Thursday with widespread winds across all waters as winds switch to the south and southwest. Once again the coastal waters will have the best chance for gusts up to storm force, while the east strait and north waters have the chance of seeing gusts up to gale force. Remaining waters will likely see small craft impacts. There will also be a 30% chance of thunderstorms with activity in the coastal waters. The ensembles favor high pressure rebuilding into the end of the week and weekend, with Friday being a break from winds before becoming breezy again next weekend.

Seas: 10-12 ft seas Monday will increase to 18 to 22 ft Tuesday through Thursday (with periods becoming longer midweek at 16 to 18 seconds). They will decrease to 10 to 12 ft Friday through the weekend. A small craft advisory is also in effect for Grays Harbor bar for rough bar conditions, which may become severe midweek as steeper seas move closer to the shoreline.
HPR

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: An active Pacific weather pattern arrives today, bringing a series of wet and progressively warmer systems across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington. Rain becomes widespread this afternoon, persisting through Thursday alongside rising snow levels and breezy conditions. A potential break in precipitation may develop late in the week as high pressure attempts to build over the region.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An active Pacific weather pattern arrives today, bringing a series of wet and progressively warmer systems across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington. Rain becomes widespread this afternoon, persisting through Thursday alongside rising snow levels and breezy conditions. A potential break in precipitation may develop late in the week as high pressure attempts to build over the region.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Sunday...An active stretch of Pacific weather settles into the Pacific Northwest today, kicking off a series of low pressure systems and atmospheric river moisture surges. Widespread rain develops across coastal areas and inland valleys by late this afternoon, keeping skies mostly cloudy throughout the week. 72-hour rain totals through Thursday morning will yield a 65-90% chance for at least 1 inch of rain along the coast, while inland valleys see a 15-50% chance of reaching that mark, with the highest totals focused north of the Columbia River. Central and eastern Lane County will see a 20-30% chance for 0.50 inches or more. Additionally, a slight chance of thunderstorms accompanies the moisture surges across the coast and interior lowlands on Wednesday night and Thanksgiving Day.

Coastal communities, beaches, and headlands will experience gusty winds alongside steady rain, with the strongest coastal winds developing after 10 PM Wednesday and continuing through Thursday. Ahead of that peak, there is a 25-55% chance of wind gusts reaching 45 mph or higher tonight into Tuesday night, followed by a 35-65% chance of gusts reaching 45 mph or higher from Tuesday night into Wednesday night. High winds along the coast develop after 10 PM Wednesday and continue through Thursday, carrying a 30-50% chance of gusts exceeding 55 mph. Through the Columbia River Gorge and parts of the east Portland metro area, easterly winds will gust between 35-50 mph starting tonight and lasting through Tuesday. There is a 50-80% chance of gusts exceeding 35 mph, and a 10-20% chance of exceeding 50 mph. Daytime high temperatures will reach the mid 50s to low 60s along the coast, and low to upper 50s in inland valleys, with overnight lows holding in the mid 40s to mid 50s at the coast and low 40s to low 50s inland.

As atmospheric moisture transport peaks mid-week, significant warming aloft will send 850 mb temperatures up to 3C to 7C. Snow levels will climb to 4500-5500 feet by Tuesday, and further increase to 6000-7500 feet by Wednesday and Thursday. Consequently, pass-level snow accumulations will remain minimal through the majority of the week due to these exceptionally high snow levels. Daytime higher temperatures in the Cascades will range from the upper 30s to upper 40s, with overnight lows in the low 30s to low 40s.

Looking ahead toward the end of the week and next weekend, model clusters show a split in solutions regarding our weather pattern. A solid majority of ensemble clusters lean toward a building high pressure ridge that would bring a welcome break in precipitation and quieter weather. However, a minority of solutions maintain unsettled troughing overhead, which would keep rain chances going. Long-range uncertainty remains high until these differing solutions converge over the coming days. ~12

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Tuesday...VFR conditions will continue across NW OR and SW WA through today. Showers will continue along the coast and Coast Range through the morning, ending around 17-19Z Mon. Pressure gradients have begun to tighten this morning, increasing winds along the eastern Portland Metro with gusts up to 25-30 kt at KTTD. Winds also have begun to increase along the coast and the Columbia River from KTTD to KVUO, resulting in gusts up to 25 kts possible. Another weather system approaches the airspace later in the TAF period, bringing widespread rain showers to the coast around 22Z Mon and inland around 01Z Tue. Current guidance does not expect conditions to deteriorate to below FL045.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...VFR through the TAF period. Easterly winds increase at KPDX through this morning with gusts to 20-25 kt possible. East of KPDX, expect gusts up to 25 kts at KTTD, increasing to up to 30 kts around 18Z Mon. ~12

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: The next storm system arrives today, increasing winds through Tuesday. Today, there is high confidence (>80% chance) for gale force wind gusts up to 40 kt across the outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore. For the inner waters and Columbia River Bar, this system appears to stay offshore enough to maintain small craft wind gusts up to 30 kt, however, can't rule out isolated gale force gusts up to 35 kt. By Tuesday, winds from this system strengthen, bringing storm force wind gusts of 50-55 kt to the outer waters, mainly beyond 30-40 NM offshore. For the inner waters and Columbia River Bar, winds increase to gale force gusts up to 40 kt. Gale Warnings are currently in effect for the outer waters, with Storm Warnings following on Tuesday. For the inner waters and Columbia River Bar, Small Craft Advisories continue through tonight before upgrading to Gale Warnings on Tuesday.

Seas will also gradually build tonight into Tuesday, peaking between 17-22 ft at 15-17 seconds Tuesday afternoon. The steepest seas are expected beyond 30 NM, where there is moderate to high confidence (50-80% chance) for seas exceeding 20 ft. For the main channel of the Columbia River Bar, chances for exceeding 20 ft remain around 5-10%. Chances are lower because seas will be primarily wind-driven rather than westerly swell- driven. Active marine conditions continue through mid-week with additional chances for gales and steep seas. ~12/10

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A Coastal Flood Advisory for tidal overflow remains in effect through 4 AM Tuesday. A Coastal Flood Advisory means that tidal overflow flooding is expected. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property.

Also, a Coastal Flood Warning has been issued as coastal flooding will be possible starting very early Tuesday morning through late Thursday night. The combination of elevated seas, kelvin waves, and a perigean tide (king tide) could result in major flooding. Coastal flood waters up to two feet above ground level along the immediate coast as well as low lying areas near bays, sloughs, and the lower reaches of the coastal rivers will be possible.

Through the upcoming week, a long period swell around 15-17 seconds combined with elevated seas up to 22 ft will result in an elevated sneaker wave threat. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.
